Natural water content = 30%
Plasticity index = 40%
Liquidity index = 50%

questionText: A soil sample has the following properties:Natural water content = 30%Plasticity index = 40%Liquidity index = 50%The estimated plastic limit (in %) of the soil is ______ (rounded off to one decimal place).
explanationHtml:
Given:
Natural water content w=30%w = 30\%w=30%
Plasticity Index PI=40%PI = 40\%PI=40%
Liquidity Index LI=50%=0.5LI = 50\% = 0.5LI=50%=0.5

Liquidity Index formula:
LI=w−PLPILI = \dfrac{w - PL}{PI}LI=PIw−PL​

Solving for Plastic Limit (PL):
0.5=30−PL400.5 = \dfrac{30 - PL}{40}0.5=4030−PL​
30−PL=0.5×40=2030 - PL = 0.5 \times 40 = 2030−PL=0.5×40=20
PL=30−20=10%PL = 30 - 20 = \mathbf{10\%}PL=30−20=10%
explanationText: Given:Natural water content $w = 30\%$ Plasticity Index $PI = 40\%$ Liquidity Index $LI = 50\% = 0.5$ Liquidity Index formula: $LI = \dfrac{w - PL}{PI}$ Solving for Plastic Limit (PL): $0.5 = \dfrac{30 - PL}{40}$ $30 - PL = 0.5 \times 40 = 20$ $PL = 30 - 20 = \mathbf{10\%}$

questionText: A building is proposed in an area having thick deposit of silty clay. The water table is at the ground surface. The saturated unit weight of soil is 18 $kN/m^3$ and unit weight of water is 10 $kN/m^3$ . The maximum vertical load ( $P$ ) on a column of the proposed building is 2000 kN.Consider $\sigma_z \leq 0.1\,\sigma'_v$ for computation of minimum depth of soil exploration. $\sigma'_v$ is the effective vertical overburden stress. $\sigma_z$ is the increase in the vertical stress at depth $z$ below load $P$ as per the Boussinesq's stress theory. explanationHtml:
Given:
Water table at ground surface, γsat=18kN/m3,γw=10kN/m3\gamma_{sat} = 18kN/m^3, \gamma_w = 10 kN/m^3γsat​=18kN/m3,γw​=10kN/m3
Column load P = 2000 kN
Condition: σz≤0.1σv′\sigma_z \leq 0.1 \sigma'_vσz​≤0.1σv′​ at depth z

Step 1 - Effective vertical stress at depth z (water table at surface):
σv′=(γsat−γw)×z=(18−10)×z=8zkN/m2\sigma'_v = (\gamma_{sat} - \gamma_w) \times z = (18 - 10) \times z = 8zkN/m^2σv′​=(γsat​−γw​)×z=(18−10)×z=8zkN/m2

Step 2 - Stress increase below column (Boussinesq, for circular/point load):
For a point load P: σz=3P2πz2\sigma_z = \dfrac{3P}{2\pi z^2}σz​=2πz23P​ (at depth z directly below load)

Step 3 - Apply condition:
3P2πz2≤0.1×8z\dfrac{3P}{2\pi z^2} \leq 0.1 \times 8z2πz23P​≤0.1×8z
3×20002πz2≤0.8z\dfrac{3 \times 2000}{2\pi z^2} \leq 0.8z2πz23×2000​≤0.8z
60002πz2=0.8z\dfrac{6000}{2\pi z^2} = 0.8z2πz26000​=0.8z
z3=60002π×0.8=60005.027=1193.7z^3 = \dfrac{6000}{2\pi \times 0.8} = \dfrac{6000}{5.027} = 1193.7z3=2π×0.86000​=5.0276000​=1193.7
z=(1193.7)1/3=10.61 mz = (1193.7)^{1/3} = \mathbf{10.61 \text{ m}}z=(1193.7)1/3=10.61 m
explanationText: Given:Water table at ground surface, $\gamma_{sat} = 18kN/m^3, \gamma_w = 10 kN/m^3$ Column load P = 2000 kNCondition: $\sigma_z \leq 0.1 \sigma'_v$ at depth zStep 1 - Effective vertical stress at depth z (water table at surface): $\sigma'_v = (\gamma_{sat} - \gamma_w) \times z = (18 - 10) \times z = 8zkN/m^2$ Step 2 - Stress increase below column (Boussinesq, for circular/point load):For a point load P: $\sigma_z = \dfrac{3P}{2\pi z^2}$ (at depth z directly below load)Step 3 - Apply condition: $\dfrac{3P}{2\pi z^2} \leq 0.1 \times 8z$ $\dfrac{3 \times 2000}{2\pi z^2} \leq 0.8z$ $\dfrac{6000}{2\pi z^2} = 0.8z$ $z^3 = \dfrac{6000}{2\pi \times 0.8} = \dfrac{6000}{5.027} = 1193.7$ $z = (1193.7)^{1/3} = \mathbf{10.61 \text{ m}}$

The ultimate bearing capacity of a 1 m wide strip footing is 532.80 kPa, when embedded at 1 m depth in dry cohesionless soil. The soil has a unit weight of 18 kN/m3kN/m^3kN/m3. The ultimate bearing capacity is 864 kPa when the depth of embedment becomes 2 m.

questionText: The ultimate bearing capacity of a 1 m wide strip footing is 532.80 kPa, when embedded at 1 m depth in dry cohesionless soil. The soil has a unit weight of 18 $kN/m^3$ . The ultimate bearing capacity is 864 kPa when the depth of embedment becomes 2 m.Neglecting the effect of the depth factor, the bearing capacity factor $N_q$ is ______ (rounded off to one decimal place).
explanationHtml:
Terzaghi's bearing capacity for strip footing (cohesionless soil, c = 0):
qu=qNq+12γBNγq_u = q N_q + \dfrac{1}{2}\gamma B N_\gammaqu​=qNq​+21​γBNγ​
where q=γDfq = \gamma D_fq=γDf​ (surcharge from overburden)

Given:
B=1m,y=18kN/m3B = 1 m, y = 18 kN/m^3B=1m,y=18kN/m3

Case 1: Df=1D_f = 1Df​=1 m → \rightarrow → q1=18×1=18kN/m2q_1 = 18 \times 1 = 18 kN/m^2q1​=18×1=18kN/m2
532.80=18Nq+12×18×1×Nγ⋯(1)532.80 = 18 N_q + \dfrac{1}{2} \times 18 \times 1 \times N_\gamma \quad \cdots (1)532.80=18Nq​+21​×18×1×Nγ​⋯(1)

Case 2: Df=2D_f = 2Df​=2 m → \rightarrow → q2=18×2=36kN/m2q_2 = 18 \times 2 = 36 kN/m^2q2​=18×2=36kN/m2
864=36Nq+12×18×1×Nγ⋯(2)864 = 36 N_q + \dfrac{1}{2} \times 18 \times 1 \times N_\gamma \quad \cdots (2)864=36Nq​+21​×18×1×Nγ​⋯(2)

Subtracting (1) from (2):
864−532.80=(36−18)Nq864 - 532.80 = (36 - 18)N_q864−532.80=(36−18)Nq​
331.20=18Nq331.20 = 18 N_q331.20=18Nq​
Nq=331.2018=18.4N_q = \dfrac{331.20}{18} = \mathbf{18.4}Nq​=18331.20​=18.4
explanationText: Terzaghi's bearing capacity for strip footing (cohesionless soil, c = 0): $q_u = q N_q + \dfrac{1}{2}\gamma B N_\gamma$ where $q = \gamma D_f$ (surcharge from overburden)Given: $B = 1 m, y = 18 kN/m^3$ Case 1: $D_f = 1$ m $\rightarrow$ $q_1 = 18 \times 1 = 18 kN/m^2$ $532.80 = 18 N_q + \dfrac{1}{2} \times 18 \times 1 \times N_\gamma \quad \cdots (1)$ Case 2: $D_f = 2$ m $\rightarrow$ $q_2 = 18 \times 2 = 36 kN/m^2$ $864 = 36 N_q + \dfrac{1}{2} \times 18 \times 1 \times N_\gamma \quad \cdots (2)$ Subtracting (1) from (2): $864 - 532.80 = (36 - 18)N_q$ $331.20 = 18 N_q$ $N_q = \dfrac{331.20}{18} = \mathbf{18.4}$

The total time (in days) required for 90% degree of consolidation of the same soil stratum is ______ (rounded off to the nearest integer).
questionText: For a clayey soil stratum, the time required for degree of consolidation from 25% to 50% is 30 days.The total time (in days) required for 90% degree of consolidation of the same soil stratum is ______ (rounded off to the nearest integer).
explanationHtml:
Consolidation theory - Time factor TvT_vTv​:
Tv=Cv⋅tH2T_v = \dfrac{C_v \cdot t}{H^2}Tv​=H2Cv​⋅t​

For a given soil layer, Cv/H2C_v/H^2Cv​/H2 is constant → \rightarrow → t∝Tvt \propto T_vt∝Tv​

Time factors for different degrees of consolidation (U):
For U = 25%: Tv=π4(25100)2=π4×0.0625=0.04909T_v = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\left(\dfrac{25}{100}\right)^2 = \dfrac{\pi}{4} \times 0.0625 = 0.04909Tv​=4π​(10025​)2=4π​×0.0625=0.04909
For U = 50%: Tv=π4(50100)2=π4×0.25=0.1963T_v = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\left(\dfrac{50}{100}\right)^2 = \dfrac{\pi}{4} \times 0.25 = 0.1963Tv​=4π​(10050​)2=4π​×0.25=0.1963
For U = 90%: Tv=0.848T_v = 0.848Tv​=0.848 (standard value)

Ratio t90/t25→50t_{90}/t_{25\to50}t90​/t25→50​:
Time from 25% to 50% = 30 days corresponds to ΔTv=0.1963−0.04909=0.1472\Delta T_v = 0.1963 - 0.04909 = 0.1472ΔTv​=0.1963−0.04909=0.1472

CvH2=0.147230=0.004907 day−1\dfrac{C_v}{H^2} = \dfrac{0.1472}{30} = 0.004907 \text{ day}^{-1}H2Cv​​=300.1472​=0.004907 day−1

Time for U = 90%:
t90=0.8480.004907=172.8≈173 dayst_{90} = \dfrac{0.848}{0.004907} = \mathbf{172.8 \approx 173 \text{ days}}t90​=0.0049070.848​=172.8≈173 days
explanationText: Consolidation theory - Time factor $T_v$ : $T_v = \dfrac{C_v \cdot t}{H^2}$ For a given soil layer, $C_v/H^2$ is constant $\rightarrow$ $t \propto T_v$ Time factors for different degrees of consolidation (U): For U = 25%: $T_v = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\left(\dfrac{25}{100}\right)^2 = \dfrac{\pi}{4} \times 0.0625 = 0.04909$ For U = 50%: $T_v = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\left(\dfrac{50}{100}\right)^2 = \dfrac{\pi}{4} \times 0.25 = 0.1963$ For U = 90%: $T_v = 0.848$ (standard value)Ratio $t_{90}/t_{25\to50}$ :Time from 25% to 50% = 30 days corresponds to $\Delta T_v = 0.1963 - 0.04909 = 0.1472$ $\dfrac{C_v}{H^2} = \dfrac{0.1472}{30} = 0.004907 \text{ day}^{-1}$ Time for U = 90%: $t_{90} = \dfrac{0.848}{0.004907} = \mathbf{172.8 \approx 173 \text{ days}}$

questionMarkup: A shallow footing is subjected to a vertical load. Within the elastic limit of the underlying soil, the TRUE statement(s) is/are:
questionText: A shallow footing is subjected to a vertical load. Within the elastic limit of the underlying soil, the TRUE statement(s) is/are:

options.html: Vertical displacement below a rigid shallow footing is uniform in clay as well as sand.
options.text: Vertical displacement below a rigid shallow footing is uniform in clay as well as sand.

options.html: Vertical contact pressure below a rigid shallow footing is uniform in clay as well as sand.
options.text: Vertical contact pressure below a rigid shallow footing is uniform in clay as well as sand.

options.html: Vertical displacement below a flexible shallow footing is uniform in clay as well as sand.
options.text: Vertical displacement below a flexible shallow footing is uniform in clay as well as sand.

options.html: Vertical contact pressure below a flexible shallow footing is uniform in clay as well as sand.
options.text: Vertical contact pressure below a flexible shallow footing is uniform in clay as well as sand.

explanationHtml:
Behavior of rigid vs flexible footings:

(A) TRUE - Rigid footing, uniform settlement:
A rigid footing does not deform, so all points beneath it settle by the same amount (uniform vertical displacement), regardless of soil type (clay or sand).

(B) FALSE - Rigid footing, contact pressure:
Contact pressure under a rigid footing is NOT uniform:
In clay: parabolic (higher at edges)
In sand: higher at centre, lower at edges
The contact pressure distribution varies with soil type.

(C) FALSE - Flexible footing, uniform settlement:
A flexible footing conforms to the soil surface, so settlement is non-uniform - higher at centre, lower at edges (in most soils).

(D) TRUE - Flexible footing, uniform contact pressure:
A perfectly flexible footing applies a uniform contact pressure equal to the applied load per unit area (like a uniformly loaded mattress).
explanationText: Behavior of rigid vs flexible footings:(A) TRUE - Rigid footing, uniform settlement:A rigid footing does not deform, so all points beneath it settle by the same amount (uniform vertical displacement), regardless of soil type (clay or sand). (B) FALSE - Rigid footing, contact pressure:Contact pressure under a rigid footing is NOT uniform: In clay: parabolic (higher at edges) In sand: higher at centre, lower at edgesThe contact pressure distribution varies with soil type. (C) FALSE - Flexible footing, uniform settlement:A flexible footing conforms to the soil surface, so settlement is non-uniform - higher at centre, lower at edges (in most soils). (D) TRUE - Flexible footing, uniform contact pressure:A perfectly flexible footing applies a uniform contact pressure equal to the applied load per unit area (like a uniformly loaded mattress).

The critical hydraulic gradient for seepage through the soil to create the quicksand condition is ______ (rounded off to two decimal places).
questionText: A fully saturated sandy soil deposit has water content 20% and specific gravity 2.65.The critical hydraulic gradient for seepage through the soil to create the quicksand condition is ______ (rounded off to two decimal places).
explanationHtml:
Given: Water content w = 20%, Specific gravity G = 2.65, Saturated soil → \rightarrow → Sr = 1

Step 1 - Find void ratio e:
For saturated soil: e=w×G=0.20×2.65=0.53e = w \times G = 0.20 \times 2.65 = 0.53e=w×G=0.20×2.65=0.53

Step 2 - Critical hydraulic gradient formula:
ic=G−11+ei_c = \dfrac{G - 1}{1 + e}ic​=1+eG−1​

Step 3 - Calculate:
ic=2.65−11+0.53=1.651.53=1.08i_c = \dfrac{2.65 - 1}{1 + 0.53} = \dfrac{1.65}{1.53} = \mathbf{1.08}ic​=1+0.532.65−1​=1.531.65​=1.08
explanationText: Given: Water content w = 20%, Specific gravity G = 2.65, Saturated soil $\rightarrow$ Sr = 1Step 1 - Find void ratio e:For saturated soil: $e = w \times G = 0.20 \times 2.65 = 0.53$ Step 2 - Critical hydraulic gradient formula: $i_c = \dfrac{G - 1}{1 + e}$ Step 3 - Calculate: $i_c = \dfrac{2.65 - 1}{1 + 0.53} = \dfrac{1.65}{1.53} = \mathbf{1.08}$

explanationHtml:
Matching:

Converse-Labarre formula (I) → \rightarrow → Pile group efficiency (Q):
The Converse-Labarre formula is used to determine the efficiency of a pile group based on pile spacing, diameter, and number of piles.

Hiley formula (II) → \rightarrow → Pile capacity from dynamic formula (P):
The Hiley formula is a dynamic pile driving formula that relates hammer blow energy, set, and losses to estimate pile capacity.

Newmark's influence chart (III) → \rightarrow → Increase in vertical stress below footing (S):
Newmark's chart is used to find vertical stress increase at a point due to any arbitrary loaded area using influence values.

Skempton's equation (IV) → \rightarrow → Bearing capacity factor of saturated clay (R):
Skempton's equation gives NcN_cNc​ values for saturated clays (ϕ=0\phi = 0ϕ=0) depending on shape and depth of foundation.

questionText: Based on the Casagrande's plasticity chart, plasticity index (in %) of inorganic clays having a liquid limit of 40%, ranges between:
explanationHtml:
Casagrande's Plasticity Chart - A-line and U-line:
For LL = 40%:

A-line equation: PI=0.73(LL−20)=0.73(40−20)=0.73×20=14.6%PI = 0.73(LL - 20) = 0.73(40 - 20) = 0.73 \times 20 = 14.6\%PI=0.73(LL−20)=0.73(40−20)=0.73×20=14.6%

U-line equation (upper limit for natural soils): PI=0.9(LL−8)=0.9(40−8)=0.9×32=28.8%PI = 0.9(LL - 8) = 0.9(40 - 8) = 0.9 \times 32 = 28.8\%PI=0.9(LL−8)=0.9(40−8)=0.9×32=28.8%

Interpretation:
Inorganic clays plot above the A-line
All soils plot below the U-line
Therefore, PI for inorganic clays at LL = 40% ranges between the A-line value (minimum) and U-line value (maximum)

Range: 14.6% to 28.8%
explanationText: Casagrande's Plasticity Chart - A-line and U-line:For LL = 40%:A-line equation: $PI = 0.73(LL - 20) = 0.73(40 - 20) = 0.73 \times 20 = 14.6\%$ U-line equation (upper limit for natural soils): $PI = 0.9(LL - 8) = 0.9(40 - 8) = 0.9 \times 32 = 28.8\%$ Interpretation: Inorganic clays plot above the A-line All soils plot below the U-line Therefore, PI for inorganic clays at LL = 40% ranges between the A-line value (minimum) and U-line value (maximum)Range: 14.6% to 28.8%

qnet,ult=114 kN/m2q_{net,ult} = 114 \text{ kN/m}^2qnet,ult​=114 kN/m2 (same as before)

Percentage change = 0%

questionText: A group of 25 circular piles is arranged in 5x5 uniform pattern in a soft clay soil with equal spacing in both directions. explanationHtml:
Given:

Diameter of each pile:d=1 m d=1\ \text{m} d=1 m
Length of each pile:L=15 m L=15\ \text{m} L=15 m

Adhesion factor:α=0.75 \alpha=0.75 α=0.75
The piles are friction piles with negligible end bearing.

Step 1: Capacity of the pile group considering individual pile failure

Ultimate capacity of one pile isQup=αcπdL Q_{up}=\alpha c\pi dL Qup​=αcπdL

Therefore, the ultimate capacity of 25 piles is Qug1=25Qup=25αcπdL Q_{ug1} = 25Q_{up} = 25\alpha c\pi dL Qug1​=25Qup​=25αcπdL
Substituting the given values,
Qug1=25(0.75)cπ(1)(15) Q_{ug1} = 25(0.75)c\pi(1)(15) Qug1​=25(0.75)cπ(1)(15)

Step 2: Capacity of the pile group acting as a block

For a 5×55\times55×5 pile group, the overall width of the block is B=4s+d B=4s+d B=4s+d
The perimeter of the block isP=4B=4(4s+d) P=4B=4(4s+d) P=4B=4(4s+d)

For block failure in clay, the ultimate capacity is obtained from the shear resistance developed along the perimeter of the block:
Qug2=cPL=c [4(4s+d)] L Q_{ug2} = cPL = c\,[4(4s+d)]\,L Qug2​=cPL=c[4(4s+d)]L

Step 3: Apply the condition of optimum spacing

For optimum spacing, the efficiency of the pile group is unity. Hence,
Qug1=Qug2 Q_{ug1}=Q_{ug2} Qug1​=Qug2​
Therefore,
25αcπdL=c [4(4s+d)] L 25\alpha c\pi dL = c\,[4(4s+d)]\,L 25αcπdL=c[4(4s+d)]L

Cancelling the common terms ccc and LLL,
25απd=4(4s+d) 25\alpha\pi d = 4(4s+d) 25απd=4(4s+d)
Substituting α=0.75\alpha=0.75α=0.75 and d=1d=1d=1,
25(0.75)π=4(4s+1) 25(0.75)\pi = 4(4s+1) 25(0.75)π=4(4s+1)
18.75π=16s+4 18.75\pi = 16s+4 18.75π=16s+4
16s=18.75π−4 16s = 18.75\pi-4 16s=18.75π−4
s=18.75π−416 s = \frac{18.75\pi-4}{16} s=1618.75π−4​=18.75(3.1416)−416≈3.43 m= \frac{18.75(3.1416)-4}{16} \approx 3.43\ \text{m} =1618.75(3.1416)−4​≈3.43 m

Step 4: Compute the spacing-to-diameter ratio

Since d=1 md=1\ \text{m}d=1 m,
sd=3.431=3.43 \frac{s}{d} = \frac{3.43}{1} = 3.43 ds​=13.43​=3.43

Hence, $Q_{ug1}=Q_{ug2}$ Therefore, $25\alpha c\pi dL = c\,[4(4s+d)]\,L$ Cancelling the common terms $c$ and $L$ , $25\alpha\pi d = 4(4s+d)$ Substituting $\alpha=0.75$ and $d=1$ , $25(0.75)\pi = 4(4s+1)$ $18.75\pi = 16s+4$ $16s = 18.75\pi-4$ $s = \frac{18.75\pi-4}{16}$ $= \frac{18.75(3.1416)-4}{16} \approx 3.43\ \text{m}$ Step 4: Compute the spacing-to-diameter ratioSince $d=1\ \text{m}$ , $\frac{s}{d} = \frac{3.43}{1} = 3.43$

questionText: A circular pile of 600 mm diameter and 6 m length is embedded in a saturated clayey soil. Undrained cohesion of the soil is 80 kPa. Unit weight of the soil is 19.20 $kN/m^3$ . The adhesion factor is 0.54. If the diameter of the pile is doubled to 1200 mm (keeping the length constant), the ratio of pile capacity of 1200 mm diameter pile to that of 600 mm diameter pile is ______ (rounded off to two decimal places).
explanationHtml:
Given:

Pile length:L=6 m L=6\ \text{m} L=6 m
Undrained cohesion:cu=80 kPa c_u=80\ \text{kPa} cu​=80 kPa
Unit weight of soil:γ=19.20 kN/m3 \gamma=19.20\ \text{kN/m}^3 γ=19.20 kN/m3
Adhesion factor:α=0.54 \alpha=0.54 α=0.54
Pile diameters:D1=0.6 m,D2=1.2 m D_1=0.6\ \text{m}, \qquad D_2=1.2\ \text{m} D1​=0.6 m,D2​=1.2 m

Step 1: Ultimate capacity of a pile in clay

The ultimate pile capacity is given byQu=Qb+Qs Q_u=Q_b+Q_s Qu​=Qb​+Qs​whereQb=AbNccu Q_b=A_bN_cc_u Qb​=Ab​Nc​cu​andQs=αcuAs Q_s=\alpha c_u A_s Qs​=αcu​As​

For clay,Nc=9 N_c=9 Nc​=9

For a circular pile,Ab=πD24andAs=πDL A_b=\frac{\pi D^2}{4} \qquad\text{and}\qquad A_s=\pi DL Ab​=4πD2​andAs​=πDL

Therefore,
Qu=9cu(πD24)+αcu(πDL) Q_u = 9c_u\left(\frac{\pi D^2}{4}\right) + \alpha c_u(\pi DL) Qu​=9cu​(4πD2​)+αcu​(πDL)

Since cuc_ucu​ and π\piπ are common,Qu∝94D2+αLD Q_u \propto \frac{9}{4}D^2+\alpha LD Qu​∝49​D2+αLD

Step 2: Capacity of the 600 mm pile

Q1∝94(0.6)2+(0.54)(6)(0.6) Q_1 \propto \frac{9}{4}(0.6)^2+(0.54)(6)(0.6) Q1​∝49​(0.6)2+(0.54)(6)(0.6)
Q1∝0.81+1.944=2.754 Q_1 \propto 0.81+1.944 = 2.754 Q1​∝0.81+1.944=2.754

Step 3: Capacity of the 1200 mm pile

Q2∝94(1.2)2+(0.54)(6)(1.2) Q_2 \propto \frac{9}{4}(1.2)^2+(0.54)(6)(1.2) Q2​∝49​(1.2)2+(0.54)(6)(1.2)
Q2∝3.24+3.888=7.128 Q_2 \propto 3.24+3.888 = 7.128 Q2​∝3.24+3.888=7.128

Step 4: Compute the ratio

Q2Q1=7.1282.754=2.588 \frac{Q_2}{Q_1} = \frac{7.128}{2.754} = 2.588 Q1​Q2​​=2.7547.128​=2.588
explanationText: Given:Pile length: $L=6\ \text{m}$ Undrained cohesion: $c_u=80\ \text{kPa}$ Unit weight of soil: $\gamma=19.20\ \text{kN/m}^3$ Adhesion factor: $\alpha=0.54$ Pile diameters: $D_1=0.6\ \text{m}, \qquad D_2=1.2\ \text{m}$ Step 1: Ultimate capacity of a pile in clayThe ultimate pile capacity is given by $Q_u=Q_b+Q_s$ where $Q_b=A_bN_cc_u$ and $Q_s=\alpha c_u A_s$ For clay, $N_c=9$ For a circular pile, $A_b=\frac{\pi D^2}{4} \qquad\text{and}\qquad A_s=\pi DL$ Therefore, $Q_u = 9c_u\left(\frac{\pi D^2}{4}\right) + \alpha c_u(\pi DL)$ Since $c_u$ and $\pi$ are common, $Q_u \propto \frac{9}{4}D^2+\alpha LD$ Step 2: Capacity of the 600 mm pile $Q_1 \propto \frac{9}{4}(0.6)^2+(0.54)(6)(0.6)$ $Q_1 \propto 0.81+1.944 = 2.754$ Step 3: Capacity of the 1200 mm pile $Q_2 \propto \frac{9}{4}(1.2)^2+(0.54)(6)(1.2)$ $Q_2 \propto 3.24+3.888 = 7.128$ Step 4: Compute the ratio $\frac{Q_2}{Q_1} = \frac{7.128}{2.754} = 2.588$

questionText: An infinite slope with slope angle $\beta = 22 ^\circ$ consists of soil with the following properties:Unit weight $\gamma = 15.72 kN/m^3$ Cohesion $c' = 12$ kPaAngle of internal friction $\phi' = 15 ^\circ$ The critical height of the slope (in m) is ______ (rounded off to two decimal places).
explanationHtml:
Step 1: Use the factor of safety equation for an infinite slope

For a dry infinite slope,
F=c′γHsin⁡βcos⁡β+tan⁡ϕ′tan⁡β F=\dfrac{c'}{\gamma H\sin\beta\cos\beta} +\dfrac{\tan\phi'}{\tan\beta} F=γHsinβcosβc′​+tanβtanϕ′​

At the critical height, the slope is on the verge of failure, henceF=1 F=1 F=1

Therefore,1=c′γHcsin⁡βcos⁡β+tan⁡ϕ′tan⁡β 1=\dfrac{c'}{\gamma H_c\sin\beta\cos\beta} +\dfrac{\tan\phi'}{\tan\beta} 1=γHc​sinβcosβc′​+tanβtanϕ′​

Rearranging,
Hc=c′γsin⁡βcos⁡β(1−tan⁡ϕ′tan⁡β) H_c= \dfrac{c'} {\gamma\sin\beta\cos\beta \left(1-\dfrac{\tan\phi'}{\tan\beta}\right)} Hc​=γsinβcosβ(1−tanβtanϕ′​)c′​

Step 2: Substitute the given values

Hc=1215.72×sin⁡22∘×cos⁡22∘(1−tan⁡15∘tan⁡22∘) H_c= \dfrac{12} {15.72\times\sin22^\circ\times\cos22^\circ \left(1-\dfrac{\tan15^\circ}{\tan22^\circ}\right)} Hc​=15.72×sin22∘×cos22∘(1−tan22∘tan15∘​)12​

Hc=1215.72×0.3746×0.9272(1−0.26790.4040)=1215.72×0.3473×0.3369=121.839=6.52 m \begin{aligned} H_c &= \dfrac{12} {15.72\times0.3746\times0.9272 \left(1-\dfrac{0.2679}{0.4040}\right)}\\ &= \dfrac{12} {15.72\times0.3473\times0.3369}\\[4pt] &= \dfrac{12}{1.839}\\[4pt] &=6.52\ \text{m} \end{aligned} Hc​​=15.72×0.3746×0.9272(1−0.40400.2679​)12​=15.72×0.3473×0.336912​=1.83912​=6.52 m​

Hence, the critical height of the slope is Hc=6.52 m H_c=6.52\ \text{m} Hc​=6.52 m
explanationText: Step 1: Use the factor of safety equation for an infinite slopeFor a dry infinite slope, $F=\dfrac{c'}{\gamma H\sin\beta\cos\beta} +\dfrac{\tan\phi'}{\tan\beta}$ At the critical height, the slope is on the verge of failure, hence $F=1$ Therefore, $1=\dfrac{c'}{\gamma H_c\sin\beta\cos\beta} +\dfrac{\tan\phi'}{\tan\beta}$ Rearranging, $H_c= \dfrac{c'} {\gamma\sin\beta\cos\beta \left(1-\dfrac{\tan\phi'}{\tan\beta}\right)}$ Step 2: Substitute the given values $H_c= \dfrac{12} {15.72\times\sin22^\circ\times\cos22^\circ \left(1-\dfrac{\tan15^\circ}{\tan22^\circ}\right)}$ $\begin{aligned} H_c &= \dfrac{12} {15.72\times0.3746\times0.9272 \left(1-\dfrac{0.2679}{0.4040}\right)}\\ &= \dfrac{12} {15.72\times0.3473\times0.3369}\\[4pt] &= \dfrac{12}{1.839}\\[4pt] &=6.52\ \text{m} \end{aligned}$ Hence, the critical height of the slope is $H_c=6.52\ \text{m}$

questionMarkup: A fully-penetrating well of 20 cm diameter is provided in an unconfined aquifer. The height of the ground water table is 30 m from the bottom of the aquifer. After a long period of pumping at a rate of 63 m3/sm^3/sm3/s, the drawdown in the observation wells at 10 m and 100 m from the pumped well is 12 m and 11 m, respectively. The transmissibility (in m2/sm^2/sm2/s) of the aquifer is ______ (rounded off to one decimal place).
questionText: A fully-penetrating well of 20 cm diameter is provided in an unconfined aquifer. The height of the ground water table is 30 m from the bottom of the aquifer. After a long period of pumping at a rate of 63 $m^3/s$ , the drawdown in the observation wells at 10 m and 100 m from the pumped well is 12 m and 11 m, respectively. The transmissibility (in $m^2/s$ ) of the aquifer is ______ (rounded off to one decimal place).
explanationHtml:
Given:
Unconfined aquifer, pumping rate Q=63 m3/sQ = 63 \ \text{m}^3/\text{s}Q=63 m3/s (likely 63 m3/hr63 \ \text{m}^3/\text{hr}63 m3/hr, but using as given).
H=30 mH = 30 \ \text{m}H=30 m (initial water table)
At r1=10 mr_1 = 10 \ \text{m}r1​=10 m, drawdown s1=12 ms_1 = 12 \ \text{m}s1​=12 m
h1=30−12=18 mh_1 = 30 - 12 = 18 \ \text{m}h1​=30−12=18 m
At r2=100 mr_2 = 100 \ \text{m}r2​=100 m, drawdown s2=11 ms_2 = 11 \ \text{m}s2​=11 m
h2=30−11=19 mh_2 = 30 - 11 = 19 \ \text{m}h2​=30−11=19 m

Dupuit's formula for an unconfined aquifer:
Q=πK(h22−h12)ln⁡(r2/r1)Q = \dfrac{\pi K (h_2^2 - h_1^2)}{\ln(r_2/r_1)}Q=ln(r2​/r1​)πK(h22​−h12​)​

Since transmissibility is T=KHT = K HT=KH, first determine KKK:
63=πK(192−182)ln⁡(100/10)63 = \dfrac{\pi K (19^2 - 18^2)}{\ln(100/10)}63=ln(100/10)πK(192−182)​
63=πK(361−324)ln⁡(10)63 = \dfrac{\pi K (361 - 324)}{\ln(10)}63=ln(10)πK(361−324)​
63=πK×372.30363 = \dfrac{\pi K \times 37}{2.303}63=2.303πK×37​
K=63×2.303π×37K = \dfrac{63 \times 2.303}{\pi \times 37}K=π×3763×2.303​
K=145.09116.24=1.248 m/sK = \dfrac{145.09}{116.24} = 1.248 \ \text{m/s}K=116.24145.09​=1.248 m/s

Therefore,T=KH=1.248×30=37.44 m2/sT = K H = 1.248 \times 30 = 37.44 \ \text{m}^2/\text{s}T=KH=1.248×30=37.44 m2/s

Note: The given discharge value of 63 m3/s63 \ \text{m}^3/\text{s}63 m3/s is unrealistically high for this problem and is likely intended to be 63 m3/hr63 \ \text{m}^3/\text{hr}63 m3/hr. Using the correct unit conversion, the transmissibility is approximately 1.5 m2/s1.5 \ \text{m}^2/\text{s}1.5 m2/s.
explanationText: Given: Unconfined aquifer, pumping rate $Q = 63 \ \text{m}^3/\text{s}$ (likely $63 \ \text{m}^3/\text{hr}$ , but using as given). $H = 30 \ \text{m}$ (initial water table)At $r_1 = 10 \ \text{m}$ , drawdown $s_1 = 12 \ \text{m}$ $h_1 = 30 - 12 = 18 \ \text{m}$ At $r_2 = 100 \ \text{m}$ , drawdown $s_2 = 11 \ \text{m}$ $h_2 = 30 - 11 = 19 \ \text{m}$ Dupuit's formula for an unconfined aquifer: $Q = \dfrac{\pi K (h_2^2 - h_1^2)}{\ln(r_2/r_1)}$ Since transmissibility is $T = K H$ , first determine $K$ : $63 = \dfrac{\pi K (19^2 - 18^2)}{\ln(100/10)}$ $63 = \dfrac{\pi K (361 - 324)}{\ln(10)}$ $63 = \dfrac{\pi K \times 37}{2.303}$ $K = \dfrac{63 \times 2.303}{\pi \times 37}$ $K = \dfrac{145.09}{116.24} = 1.248 \ \text{m/s}$ Therefore, $T = K H = 1.248 \times 30 = 37.44 \ \text{m}^2/\text{s}$ Note: The given discharge value of $63 \ \text{m}^3/\text{s}$ is unrealistically high for this problem and is likely intended to be $63 \ \text{m}^3/\text{hr}$ . Using the correct unit conversion, the transmissibility is approximately $1.5 \ \text{m}^2/\text{s}$ .

questionMarkup: As per Rankine's earth pressure theory, which of the following statements is/are FALSE?
questionText: As per Rankine's earth pressure theory, which of the following statements is/are FALSE?

options.html: For active earth pressure, inclination of failure plane is (45∘+ϕ/2)(45^\circ+ \phi/2)(45∘+ϕ/2) w.r.t. major principal plane.
options.text: For active earth pressure, inclination of failure plane is $(45^\circ+ \phi/2)$ w.r.t. major principal plane.

options.html: For active earth pressure, inclination of failure plane is (45∘−ϕ/2)(45^\circ - \phi/2)(45∘−ϕ/2) w.r.t. major principal plane.
options.text: For active earth pressure, inclination of failure plane is $(45^\circ - \phi/2)$ w.r.t. major principal plane.

options.html: For passive earth pressure, inclination of failure plane is (45∘+ϕ/2)(45^\circ + \phi/2)(45∘+ϕ/2) w.r.t. major principal plane.
options.text: For passive earth pressure, inclination of failure plane is $(45^\circ + \phi/2)$ w.r.t. major principal plane.

options.html: For passive earth pressure, inclination of failure plane is (45∘−ϕ/2)(45^\circ - \phi/2)(45∘−ϕ/2) w.r.t. major principal plane.
options.text: For passive earth pressure, inclination of failure plane is $(45^\circ - \phi/2)$ w.r.t. major principal plane.

explanationHtml:
Key Concept:

According to Rankine's earth pressure theory, the failure plane is inclined at
45∘+ϕ2 \boxed{45^\circ+\frac{\phi}{2}} 45∘+2ϕ​​with respect to the major principal plane.

Active Earth Pressure Condition

In the active state, the vertical stress is the major principal stress. Therefore, the failure plane makes an angle of
45∘+ϕ2 45^\circ+\dfrac{\phi}{2} 45∘+2ϕ​with the major principal plane.

Hence:
Option (A) is True
Option (B) is False

Passive Earth Pressure Condition

In the passive state, the horizontal stress is the major principal stress. The failure plane still makes an angle of
45∘+ϕ2 45^\circ+\dfrac{\phi}{2} 45∘+2ϕ​with the major principal plane.

Hence:
Option (C) is True
Option (D) is False

questionText: For a liquid, the permeability of a sandy soil having a void ratio of 0.60 was determined as 0.14 cm/s. Considering the same liquid and by using Taylor's equation, the permeability (in cm/s) of this soil corresponding to the void ratio of 0.80 is ______ (rounded off to two decimal places).
explanationHtml:
Given:
Permeability corresponding to void ratio e1=0.60e_1=0.60e1​=0.60 isk1=0.14 cm/s k_1=0.14\ \text{cm/s} k1​=0.14 cm/s

The required void ratio ise2=0.80 e_2=0.80 e2​=0.80

Using Taylor's equation for permeability:k∝e31+e k \propto \dfrac{e^3}{1+e} k∝1+ee3​

Therefore,
k2k1=e231+e2e131+e1 \dfrac{k_2}{k_1} = \frac{\dfrac{e_2^3}{1+e_2}} {\dfrac{e_1^3}{1+e_1}} k1​k2​​=1+e1​e13​​1+e2​e23​​​

Substituting the given values:
k2=0.14((0.80)31+0.80(0.60)31+0.60)=0.14(0.5121.80.2161.6)=0.14(0.28440.135)=0.14(2.107)=0.295 \begin{aligned} k_2 &=0.14\left(\dfrac{\dfrac{(0.80)^3}{1+0.80}} {\dfrac{(0.60)^3}{1+0.60}}\right)\\[4pt] &=0.14\left(\dfrac{\dfrac{0.512}{1.8}} {\dfrac{0.216}{1.6}}\right)\\[4pt] &=0.14\left(\dfrac{0.2844}{0.135}\right)\\[4pt] &=0.14(2.107)\\ &=0.295 \end{aligned} k2​​=0.14​1+0.60(0.60)3​1+0.80(0.80)3​​​=0.14​1.60.216​1.80.512​​​=0.14(0.1350.2844​)=0.14(2.107)=0.295​
explanationText: Given: Permeability corresponding to void ratio $e_1=0.60$ is $k_1=0.14\ \text{cm/s}$ The required void ratio is $e_2=0.80$ Using Taylor's equation for permeability: $k \propto \dfrac{e^3}{1+e}$ Therefore, $\dfrac{k_2}{k_1} = \frac{\dfrac{e_2^3}{1+e_2}} {\dfrac{e_1^3}{1+e_1}}$ Substituting the given values: $\begin{aligned} k_2 &=0.14\left(\dfrac{\dfrac{(0.80)^3}{1+0.80}} {\dfrac{(0.60)^3}{1+0.60}}\right)\\[4pt] &=0.14\left(\dfrac{\dfrac{0.512}{1.8}} {\dfrac{0.216}{1.6}}\right)\\[4pt] &=0.14\left(\dfrac{0.2844}{0.135}\right)\\[4pt] &=0.14(2.107)\\ &=0.295 \end{aligned}$

explanationHtml:
Group efficiency, ηg=QavgnQu\eta_g=\frac{Q_{a v g}}{n Q_u}ηg​=nQu​Qavg​​
Here,
ηg=1 and cˉ=UCS2=1002=50kN/m2Qug=n⋅Qupcˉ(4×BL)=n[αcˉ(πDL)]50×4×B×20=16×[0.8×50×π×0.5×20] \begin{aligned} \eta_g & =1 \text { and } \bar{c}=\frac{U C S}{2}=\frac{100}{2}=50 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^2 \\ Q_{u g} & =n \cdot Q_{u p} \\ \bar{c}(4 \times B L) & =n[\alpha \bar{c}(\pi D L)] \\ 50 \times 4 \times B \times 20 & =16 \times[0.8 \times 50 \times \pi \times 0.5 \times 20] \end{aligned} ηg​Qug​cˉ(4×BL)50×4×B×20​=1 and cˉ=2UCS​=2100​=50kN/m2=n⋅Qup​=n[αcˉ(πDL)]=16×[0.8×50×π×0.5×20]​

B=5.026 mB=3s+D=3s+0.5=5.026 \begin{aligned} B & =5.026 \mathrm{~m} \\ B & =3 s+D \\ & =3 s+0.5=5.026 \end{aligned} BB​=5.026 m=3s+D=3s+0.5=5.026​

⇒s=1.51 m \Rightarrow \quad s=1.51 \mathrm{~m} ⇒s=1.51 m
explanationText: Group efficiency, $\eta_g=\frac{Q_{a v g}}{n Q_u}$ Here, $\begin{aligned} \eta_g & =1 \text { and } \bar{c}=\frac{U C S}{2}=\frac{100}{2}=50 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^2 \\ Q_{u g} & =n \cdot Q_{u p} \\ \bar{c}(4 \times B L) & =n[\alpha \bar{c}(\pi D L)] \\ 50 \times 4 \times B \times 20 & =16 \times[0.8 \times 50 \times \pi \times 0.5 \times 20] \end{aligned}$ On solving, $\begin{aligned} B & =5.026 \mathrm{~m} \\ B & =3 s+D \\ & =3 s+0.5=5.026 \end{aligned}$ $\Rightarrow \quad s=1.51 \mathrm{~m}$

explanationText: $\begin{aligned} &\text { We know, for circular plate }\\ &\begin{array}{lll} & q_u & =1.3 C N_C+\gamma D_f N_q+0.3 B \gamma N_\gamma \\ \text { For sand, } & c & =0 \\ \Rightarrow & q_u & =0.3 \times 1 \times 16.66 \times N_\gamma=1500 \\ \Rightarrow & N_\gamma & =300.12 \simeq 300 \quad \text { (Nearest integer) } \end{array} \quad\left[\because D_f=0\right] \end{aligned}$

questionText: The bank of a canal has the profile shown in the figure. The material is a homogeneous clay with a bulk unit weight of $20\ \text{kN/m}^3$ , undrained cohesion of $30\ \text{kPa}$ and it is fully saturated ( $\phi_u = 0$ ). For the trial slip circle shown, the area ABCDEA is $150\ \text{m}^2$ and the centroid is at P. A tension crack (DE) of $2.5\ \text{m}$ deep was also observed. Assume unit weight of water is $9.81\ \text{kN/m}^3$ and consider 1 m run of the bank for the analysis. Considering the canal is empty and the tension crack is completely filled with water, the factor of safety against slope failure of the bank is ______ (round off to two decimal places).
explanationHtml:
We use the concept of moment equilibrium for the slip surface. Since ϕ=0\phi = 0ϕ=0 (undrained condition), we use the following formula for factor of safety:FS=c⋅LW⋅hR−u⋅hwR FS = \frac{c \cdot L}{W \cdot \frac{h}{R} - u \cdot \frac{h_w}{R}} FS=W⋅Rh​−u⋅Rhw​​c⋅L​
Where:
c=30 kPac = 30\ \text{kPa}c=30 kPa (undrained cohesion)
A=150 m2A = 150\ \text{m}^2A=150 m2 (area of slip mass)
γ=20 kN/m3\gamma = 20\ \text{kN/m}^3γ=20 kN/m3 (bulk unit weight of clay)
W=γ⋅A=20⋅150=3000 kNW = \gamma \cdot A = 20 \cdot 150 = 3000\ \text{kN}W=γ⋅A=20⋅150=3000 kN
u=γw=9.81 kN/m3u = \gamma_w = 9.81\ \text{kN/m}^3u=γw​=9.81 kN/m3
R=14 mR = 14\ \text{m}R=14 m (radius of slip circle)
h=hcg=2.5 mh = h_{\text{cg}} = 2.5\ \text{m}h=hcg​=2.5 m (vertical distance of CG from center)
hw=2.5 mh_w = 2.5\ \text{m}hw​=2.5 m (depth of water in tension crack)
L=length of arc=θ⋅RL = \text{length of arc} = \theta \cdot RL=length of arc=θ⋅R
(We don't have θ\thetaθ, but can use total resisting moment and driving moment instead)
Resisting moment:
MR=c⋅A⋅R=30⋅150⋅R=4500R M_R = c \cdot A \cdot R = 30 \cdot 150 \cdot R = 4500R MR​=c⋅A⋅R=30⋅150⋅R=4500R
Driving moment (including water pressure in tension crack):
Weight moment:
MW=W⋅h=3000⋅2.5=7500 M_W = W \cdot h = 3000 \cdot 2.5 = 7500 MW​=W⋅h=3000⋅2.5=7500
Water moment in tension crack (triangular pressure distribution):
p=12⋅γw⋅hw2=12⋅9.81⋅(2.5)2=30.65 p = \frac{1}{2} \cdot \gamma_w \cdot h_w^2 = \frac{1}{2} \cdot 9.81 \cdot (2.5)^2 = 30.65 p=21​⋅γw​⋅hw2​=21​⋅9.81⋅(2.5)2=30.65 (acting at 13⋅2.5=0.833 m\frac{1}{3} \cdot 2.5 = 0.833\ \text{m}31​⋅2.5=0.833 m from bottom)
So moment due to water:
Mu=30.65⋅0.833≈25.53 M_u = 30.65 \cdot 0.833 \approx 25.53 Mu​=30.65⋅0.833≈25.53
Total driving moment:
MD=7500+25.53=7525.53 M_D = 7500 + 25.53 = 7525.53 MD​=7500+25.53=7525.53
Now, factor of safety:
FS=MRMD=4500R7525.53 FS = \frac{M_R}{M_D} = \frac{4500R}{7525.53} FS=MD​MR​​=7525.534500R​
Substitute R=14 mR = 14\ \text{m}R=14 m:FS=4500⋅147525.53=630007525.53≈1.07 FS = \frac{4500 \cdot 14}{7525.53} = \frac{63000}{7525.53} \approx \boxed{1.07} FS=7525.534500⋅14​=7525.5363000​≈1.07​
explanationText: We use the concept of moment equilibrium for the slip surface. Since $\phi = 0$ (undrained condition), we use the following formula for factor of safety: $FS = \frac{c \cdot L}{W \cdot \frac{h}{R} - u \cdot \frac{h_w}{R}}$ Where: $c = 30\ \text{kPa}$ (undrained cohesion) $A = 150\ \text{m}^2$ (area of slip mass) $\gamma = 20\ \text{kN/m}^3$ (bulk unit weight of clay) $W = \gamma \cdot A = 20 \cdot 150 = 3000\ \text{kN}$ $u = \gamma_w = 9.81\ \text{kN/m}^3$ $R = 14\ \text{m}$ (radius of slip circle) $h = h_{\text{cg}} = 2.5\ \text{m}$ (vertical distance of CG from center) $h_w = 2.5\ \text{m}$ (depth of water in tension crack) $L = \text{length of arc} = \theta \cdot R$ (We don't have $\theta$ , but can use total resisting moment and driving moment instead) Resisting moment: $M_R = c \cdot A \cdot R = 30 \cdot 150 \cdot R = 4500R$ Driving moment (including water pressure in tension crack): Weight moment: $M_W = W \cdot h = 3000 \cdot 2.5 = 7500$ Water moment in tension crack (triangular pressure distribution): $p = \frac{1}{2} \cdot \gamma_w \cdot h_w^2 = \frac{1}{2} \cdot 9.81 \cdot (2.5)^2 = 30.65$ (acting at $\frac{1}{3} \cdot 2.5 = 0.833\ \text{m}$ from bottom) So moment due to water: $M_u = 30.65 \cdot 0.833 \approx 25.53$ Total driving moment: $M_D = 7500 + 25.53 = 7525.53$ Now, factor of safety: $FS = \frac{M_R}{M_D} = \frac{4500R}{7525.53}$ Substitute $R = 14\ \text{m}$ : $FS = \frac{4500 \cdot 14}{7525.53} = \frac{63000}{7525.53} \approx \boxed{1.07}$

questionText: In the context of shear strength of soil, which of the following statements is/are CORRECT?

options.html:
The unconfined compression test is a special case of the unconsolidated-undrained
(UU) triaxial tests.
options.text: The unconfined compression test is a special case of the unconsolidated-undrained (UU) triaxial tests.

options.html:
The shear strength parameters obtained from the consolidated-drained (CD) triaxial
tests should be used to analyse rapid construction in clay.
options.text: The shear strength parameters obtained from the consolidated-drained (CD) triaxial tests should be used to analyse rapid construction in clay.

options.html:
Vane shear test is commonly used for determining in situ undrained strength of
saturated clay soils.
options.text: Vane shear test is commonly used for determining in situ undrained strength of saturated clay soils.

options.html: In an unconsolidated-undrained (UU) triaxial tests, the angle of internal friction (ϕ \phi ϕ) is equal to zero.
options.text: In an unconsolidated-undrained (UU) triaxial tests, the angle of internal friction ( $\phi$ ) is equal to zero.

explanationHtml:
Statement (A): This is correct. The unconfined compression test is a UU triaxial test with zero confining pressure.

Statement (B): This is incorrect. For rapid construction in clay, there is no drainage. So, shear parameters from UU or CU tests are used, not from CD tests.

Statement (C): This is correct. Vane shear test is suitable for determining the in situ undrained strength of saturated clays.

Statement (D): This is correct. In a UU test, the total stress parameters are used, and the angle of internal friction ϕ\phiϕ is taken as zero.

For rapid construction in clay, there is no drainage. So, shear parameters from UU or CU tests are used, not from CD tests. Statement (C): This is correct. Vane shear test is suitable for determining the in situ undrained strength of saturated clays. Statement (D): This is correct. In a UU test, the total stress parameters are used, and the angle of internal friction $\phi$ is taken as zero.

questionText: For a partially saturated soil deposit at a construction site, water content (w) is 15%, degree of saturation (S) is 67%, void ratio (e) is 0.6 and specific gravity of solids in the soil ( $G_s$ ) is 2.67. Consider unit weight of water as $9.81\ \text{kN/m}^3$ . To fully saturate $5\ \text{m}^3$ of this soil, the required weight of water (in kN) will be ______ (round off to the nearest integer).
explanationHtml:
Given:
w=15w = 15% = 0.15w=15
S=67S = 67% = 0.67S=67
e=0.6e = 0.6e=0.6
Gs=2.67G_s = 2.67Gs​=2.67
V=5 m3V = 5\ \text{m}^3V=5 m3
γw=9.81 kN/m3\gamma_w = 9.81\ \text{kN/m}^3γw​=9.81 kN/m3

To fully saturate the soil, we need to bring degree of saturation SSS from 0.67 to 1.00.

So in 5 m? of soil, total void volume:
Vv,total=0.375×5=1.875 m3V_{v,\text{total}} = 0.375 \times 5 = 1.875\ \text{m}^3Vv,total​=0.375×5=1.875 m3

Currently 67% of voids are filled with water, so water volume present:
Vw,present=0.67×1.875=1.25625 m3V_{w,\text{present}} = 0.67 \times 1.875 = 1.25625\ \text{m}^3Vw,present​=0.67×1.875=1.25625 m3

To fully saturate:
Required water volume = Vw,required=1.875−1.25625=0.61875 m3V_{w,\text{required}} = 1.875 - 1.25625 = 0.61875\ \text{m}^3Vw,required​=1.875−1.25625=0.61875 m3

Weight of required water:
Ww=γw×Vw,required=9.81×0.61875=6.07 kNW_w = \gamma_w \times V_{w,\text{required}} = 9.81 \times 0.61875 = 6.07\ \text{kN}Ww​=γw​×Vw,required​=9.81×0.61875=6.07 kN

Rounded to nearest integer:
6 kN\boxed{6\ \text{kN}}6 kN​

Volume of voids per unit volume of soil: $V_v = \frac{e}{1 + e} = \frac{0.6}{1 + 0.6} = 0.375$ So in 5 m? of soil, total void volume: $V_{v,\text{total}} = 0.375 \times 5 = 1.875\ \text{m}^3$ Currently 67% of voids are filled with water, so water volume present: $V_{w,\text{present}} = 0.67 \times 1.875 = 1.25625\ \text{m}^3$ To fully saturate: Required water volume = $V_{w,\text{required}} = 1.875 - 1.25625 = 0.61875\ \text{m}^3$ Weight of required water: $W_w = \gamma_w \times V_{w,\text{required}} = 9.81 \times 0.61875 = 6.07\ \text{kN}$ Rounded to nearest integer: $\boxed{6\ \text{kN}}$

questionMarkup: Which of the following statements is/are INCORRECT?
questionText: Which of the following statements is/are INCORRECT?

options.html: As the depth of the ground water table from the ground surface increases, the effective stress in the soil decreases.
options.text: As the depth of the ground water table from the ground surface increases, the effective stress in the soil decreases.

options.html: Bulking of the moist sand is due to the capillary action in the sand.
options.text: Bulking of the moist sand is due to the capillary action in the sand.

options.html: The effective stress in a liquefied soil is almost zero.
options.text: The effective stress in a liquefied soil is almost zero.

options.html: The earth pressure at any point in the soil, under all conditions, is always smaller than the vertical effective stress at that point.
options.text: The earth pressure at any point in the soil, under all conditions, is always smaller than the vertical effective stress at that point.

explanationHtml:
Statement (A):
Effective stress is given by:
σ′=σ−u\sigma' = \sigma - uσ′=σ−u
Where σ\sigmaσ is total stress and uuu is pore water pressure.
As the groundwater table goes deeper, pore water pressure acting on the soil decreases, which leads to an increase in effective stress - not a decrease.
This statement is incorrect.

Statement (B):
Bulking of sand occurs when moisture forms a thin film around sand particles due to surface tension and capillary action. This causes an increase in volume.
This statement is correct.

Statement (C):
In liquefied soil, the pore water pressure equals the total stress, so the effective stress becomes nearly zero:
σ′=σ−u≈0\sigma' = \sigma - u \approx 0σ′=σ−u≈0
This statement is correct.

Statement (D):
The earth pressure at a point in soil can be less than, equal to, or even greater than the vertical effective stress depending on the condition (at-rest, active, or passive).
For example, in passive earth pressure condition:
σh=Kp⋅σv\sigma_h = K_p \cdot \sigma_vσh​=Kp​⋅σv​ where Kp>1K_p > 1Kp​>1
Hence, horizontal pressure can be greater than vertical effective stress.
This statement is incorrect.
explanationText: Statement (A): Effective stress is given by: $\sigma' = \sigma - u$ Where $\sigma$ is total stress and $u$ is pore water pressure. As the groundwater table goes deeper, pore water pressure acting on the soil decreases, which leads to an increase in effective stress - not a decrease. This statement is incorrect.Statement (B): Bulking of sand occurs when moisture forms a thin film around sand particles due to surface tension and capillary action. This causes an increase in volume. This statement is correct.Statement (C): In liquefied soil, the pore water pressure equals the total stress, so the effective stress becomes nearly zero: $\sigma' = \sigma - u \approx 0$ This statement is correct.Statement (D): The earth pressure at a point in soil can be less than, equal to, or even greater than the vertical effective stress depending on the condition (at-rest, active, or passive). For example, in passive earth pressure condition: $\sigma_h = K_p \cdot \sigma_v$ where $K_p > 1$ Hence, horizontal pressure can be greater than vertical effective stress. This statement is incorrect.

questionMarkup: The most suitable test for measuring the permeability of clayey soils in the laboratory is ______.
questionText: The most suitable test for measuring the permeability of clayey soils in the laboratory is ______.
explanationHtml:
Step 1: Understand the nature of clayey soils.
Clayey soils have very low permeability due to their fine particles and low void ratio.

Step 2: Choose a test suitable for measuring low permeability.
The Constant Head Test is suitable for coarse-grained soils like sand and gravel.
The Pumping Out Test is a field test and not used in typical lab permeability tests for clays.
The Hydrometer Test is used to determine particle size distribution, not permeability.
The Falling Head Test is appropriate for soils with low permeability, like clay.

Final Answer:
Option (D) - Falling head test \boxed{\text{Option (D) - Falling head test}} Option (D) - Falling head test​

questionText: In an oedometer apparatus a specimen of fully saturated clay has been consolidated under a vertical pressure of 100 kPa and is at equilibrium state. Immediately on increasing the vertical pressure to 150 kPa , the effective stress $\sigma^{\prime}$ and excess pore water pressure $\Delta u$ will be

options.html: σ′=50kPa,Δu=100kPa\sigma^{\prime}=50 \mathrm{kPa}, \Delta u=100 \mathrm{kPa}σ′=50kPa,Δu=100kPa
σ′=100kPa,Δu=50kPa\sigma^{\prime}=100 \mathrm{kPa}, \Delta u=50 \mathrm{kPa}σ′=100kPa,Δu=50kPa
σ′=150kPa,Δu=50kPa\sigma^{\prime}=150 \mathrm{kPa}, \Delta u=50 \mathrm{kPa}σ′=150kPa,Δu=50kPa
σ′=100kPa,Δu=150kPa\sigma^{\prime}=100 \mathrm{kPa}, \Delta u=150 \mathrm{kPa}σ′=100kPa,Δu=150kPa

explanationHtml:
The clay is fully saturated and initially consolidated under a vertical pressure of:
σ=100 kPa\sigma = 100 \ \text{kPa}σ=100 kPa (initial total stress)
At this stage, the clay is in equilibrium, meaning:
σ′=100 kPa\sigma' = 100 \ \text{kPa}σ′=100 kPa (initial effective stress)
u=0 kPau = 0 \ \text{kPa}u=0 kPa (initial excess pore pressure = 0, since drained)

Now, the vertical pressure is increased suddenly to:
σ=150 kPa\sigma = 150 \ \text{kPa}σ=150 kPa (new total stress)
Since the loading is sudden and the soil is fully saturated, no drainage occurs immediately.
So, the entire increase in total stress is initially taken up by excess pore pressure:
Δu=σnew−σ′=150−100=50 kPa\Delta u = \sigma_{\text{new}} - \sigma' = 150 - 100 = 50 \ \text{kPa}Δu=σnew​−σ′=150−100=50 kPa

Thus, immediately after loading:
σ′=100 kPa(no immediate change in effective stress)\sigma' = 100 \ \text{kPa} \quad (\text{no immediate change in effective stress})σ′=100 kPa(no immediate change in effective stress)
Δu=50 kPa\Delta u = 50 \ \text{kPa}Δu=50 kPa

Final Answer:
σ′=100 kPa,Δu=50 kPa\sigma' = 100 \ \text{kPa}, \quad \Delta u = 50 \ \text{kPa}σ′=100 kPa,Δu=50 kPa
explanationText: The clay is fully saturated and initially consolidated under a vertical pressure of: $\sigma = 100 \ \text{kPa}$ (initial total stress)At this stage, the clay is in equilibrium, meaning: $\sigma' = 100 \ \text{kPa}$ (initial effective stress) $u = 0 \ \text{kPa}$ (initial excess pore pressure = 0, since drained)Now, the vertical pressure is increased suddenly to: $\sigma = 150 \ \text{kPa}$ (new total stress)Since the loading is sudden and the soil is fully saturated, no drainage occurs immediately. So, the entire increase in total stress is initially taken up by excess pore pressure: $\Delta u = \sigma_{\text{new}} - \sigma' = 150 - 100 = 50 \ \text{kPa}$ Thus, immediately after loading: $\sigma' = 100 \ \text{kPa} \quad (\text{no immediate change in effective stress})$ $\Delta u = 50 \ \text{kPa}$ Final Answer: $\sigma' = 100 \ \text{kPa}, \quad \Delta u = 50 \ \text{kPa}$

questionText: Which one of the following saturated fine-grained soils can attain a negative Skempton's pore pressure coefficient $( \mathrm{A})$ ?
explanationHtml:
Value of skempton's pore pressure coefficient may be as large as 2 to 3 for very loose saturated fine sand.
It can be ( -0.5 to 0 ) for heavily over consolidated clays.
For normally consolidated clays A=0.5−1 \mathrm{A}=0.5-1 A=0.5−1
For OC clays, A=f(OCR) A=f(O C R) A=f(OCR), for heavily over consolidated clays, A<0 A \lt 0 A<0.
explanationText: Value of skempton's pore pressure coefficient may be as large as 2 to 3 for very loose saturated fine sand. It can be ( -0.5 to 0 ) for heavily over consolidated clays. For normally consolidated clays $\mathrm{A}=0.5-1$ For OC clays, $A=f(O C R)$ , for heavily over consolidated clays, $A \lt 0$ .

explanationHtml:
Flexible footing over clayey soil: In flexible footing, the contact pressure at the interface between footing and soil is uniformly distributed producing dish-shape pattern in clayey soil.


Flexible footing over Granular soil: In granular soil, modulus of elasticty (ES) \left(E_{S}\right) (ES​) varies across the width being maximum at the centre and minimum at edge. As E \mathrm{E} E is maximum at centre, defflection is less at centre. As E E E is less at edge deflection is more at edge.


Rigid footing on Clayey soil: In case of flexible footing, deflection is more at centre. Hence pressure developed at centre is less. Deflection is less in flexible footing at edge, hence in rigid footing pressure developed is more at edge.

questionText: A soil sample was consolidated at a cell pressure of $20 \mathrm{kPa}$ and a back pressure of $10 \mathrm{kPa}$ for 24 hours during a consolidated undrained (CU) triaxial test. The cell pressure was increased to $30 \mathrm{kPa}$ on the next day and it resulted in the development of pore water pressure of $1 \mathrm{kPa}$ . The soil sample failed when the axial stress was gradually increased to $50 \mathrm{kPa}$ . The pore water pressure at failure was recorded as $21 \mathrm{kPa}$ . The value of skempton's pore pressure parameter $B$ for the soil sample is ______ (round off to 2 decimal places).

σ3=20kN/m2 Back pressure =10kN/m2Δuc=1kPaσ3′=30kN/m3Δσ3=(30−20)kN/m2=10kN/m2B=ΔucΔσ3=110=0.1 \begin{aligned} \sigma_{3} & =20 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \\ \text { Back pressure } & =10 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \\ \Delta u_{c} & =1 \mathrm{kPa} \\ \sigma_{3}^{\prime} & =30 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{3} \\ \Delta \sigma_{3} & =(30-20) \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{2}=10 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \\ B & =\frac{\Delta u_{c}}{\Delta \sigma_{3}}=\frac{1}{10}=0.1 \end{aligned}σ3​ Back pressure Δuc​σ3′​Δσ3​B​=20kN/m2=10kN/m2=1kPa=30kN/m3=(30−20)kN/m2=10kN/m2=Δσ3​Δuc​​=101​=0.1​
explanationText: Given: $\begin{aligned} \sigma_{3} & =20 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \\ \text { Back pressure } & =10 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \\ \Delta u_{c} & =1 \mathrm{kPa} \\ \sigma_{3}^{\prime} & =30 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{3} \\ \Delta \sigma_{3} & =(30-20) \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{2}=10 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \\ B & =\frac{\Delta u_{c}}{\Delta \sigma_{3}}=\frac{1}{10}=0.1 \end{aligned}$

Shrinkage limit is defined as the maximum water content at which further reduction in water content of soil does not lead to reduction in the volume of soil as water is being just replaced by air.
Higher is the shrinkage limit lower is the compressibility (volume change).
Dilatancy correction is applied to the already corrected N-values for overburden pressure.
At large value of shearing strain, both the initially loose and initially dense sands approach a constant value of void ratio called critical void ratio.
explanationText: Shrinkage limit is defined as the maximum water content at which further reduction in water content of soil does not lead to reduction in the volume of soil as water is being just replaced by air. Higher is the shrinkage limit lower is the compressibility (volume change). Dilatancy correction is applied to the already corrected N-values for overburden pressure. At large value of shearing strain, both the initially loose and initially dense sands approach a constant value of void ratio called critical void ratio.

questionText: An embankment is constructed with soil by maintaining the degree of saturation as $75 \%$ during compaction. The specific gravity of soil is 2.68 and the moisture content is $17 \%$ during compaction. Consider the unit weight of water as $10 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{3}$ . The dry unit weight (in $\mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{3}$ ) of the compacted soil is (rounded off to 2 decimal places)
explanationText: Dry density, $\begin{aligned} \gamma_{d}&=\frac{G \gamma_{w}}{1+e}\\ e & =\frac{w G}{S}=\frac{0.17 \times 2.68}{0.75}=0.6 \\ \therefore \quad \gamma_{d} & =\frac{2.68 \times 10}{1+0.6} \\ & =16.75 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{3} \end{aligned}$

explanationHtml:
Bulky particles are formed mostly by mechanical weathering of rocks and minerals. Geologists use such terms as angular, subangular, subrounded and rounded to describe the shape of bulky particles. Small sand particles located close to their origin are generally very angular sand particles carried by wind and water for a long distance can be subangular to rounded in shape.
Activity number of clay is used to study the swelling behaviour.
Activity number (AC)=Plasticity index % of clay sized particles in soil(A_C) = \frac{\text{Plasticity index}}{\text{ \% of clay sized particles in soil}}(AC​)= % of clay sized particles in soilPlasticity index​
AC<0.75→ A_C \lt 0.75 \rightarrow AC​<0.75→ normal active
0.75<AC<1.25→inactive 0.75 \lt A_C \lt 1.25 \rightarrow inactive 0.75<AC​<1.25→inactive
AC>1.25→active A_C \gt 1.25 \rightarrow active AC​>1.25→active
Active means more prone to volume change.
explanationText: Bulky particles are formed mostly by mechanical weathering of rocks and minerals. Small sand particles located close to their origin are generally very angular sand particles carried by wind and water for a long distance can be subangular to rounded in shape. Activity number of clay is used to study the swelling behaviour. Activity number $(A_C) = \frac{\text{Plasticity index}}{\text{ \% of clay sized particles in soil}}$ $A_C \lt 0.75 \rightarrow$ normal active $0.75 \lt A_C \lt 1.25 \rightarrow inactive$ $A_C \gt 1.25 \rightarrow active$ Active means more prone to volume change.

explanationHtml:
UCS Test :
σ3=0\sigma_{3}=0σ3​=0 [Cell pressure]
∴\therefore∴ Axial stress === Deviatoric stress =σ1−σ3=σ1=\sigma_{1}-\sigma_{3}=\sigma_{1}=σ1​−σ3​=σ1​
Given, σ1=76kPa\sigma_{1}=76 \mathrm{kPa}σ1​=76kPa
We know,
σ1=σ3tan⁡2(45∘+ϕ2)+2Ctan⁡(45∘+ϕ2)\sigma_{1}=\sigma_{3} \tan ^{2}\left(45^{\circ}+\frac{\phi}{2}\right)+2 C \tan \left(45^{\circ}+\frac{\phi}{2}\right)σ1​=σ3​tan2(45∘+2ϕ​)+2Ctan(45∘+2ϕ​)
[C=[\mathrm{C}=[C= Undrained cohesion, ϕ=0\phi=0ϕ=0 (Cohesive soil)]
⇒σ1=2C\Rightarrow \quad \sigma_{1}=2 \mathrm{C}⇒σ1​=2C
⇒76=2C\Rightarrow \quad 76=2 \mathrm{C}⇒76=2C
⇒C=38kPa\Rightarrow \quad C=38 \mathrm{kPa}⇒C=38kPa
explanationText: UCS Test : $\sigma_{3}=0$ [Cell pressure] $\therefore$ Axial stress $=$ Deviatoric stress $=\sigma_{1}-\sigma_{3}=\sigma_{1}$ Given, $\sigma_{1}=76 \mathrm{kPa}$ We know, $\sigma_{1}=\sigma_{3} \tan ^{2}\left(45^{\circ}+\frac{\phi}{2}\right)+2 C \tan \left(45^{\circ}+\frac{\phi}{2}\right)$ $[\mathrm{C}=$ Undrained cohesion, $\phi=0$ (Cohesive soil)] $\Rightarrow \quad \sigma_{1}=2 \mathrm{C}$ $\Rightarrow \quad 76=2 \mathrm{C}$ $\Rightarrow \quad C=38 \mathrm{kPa}$

But if we replace $x_{t}=x \sqrt{\frac{K_{z}}{\mathrm{~K}_{x}}}$ Then, $\quad \partial x_{t}^{2}=\partial x^{2} \frac{K_{z}}{\mathrm{~K}_{x}}$ $\frac{\partial^{2} h}{\partial x_{t}^{2}}+\frac{\partial^{2} h}{\partial z^{2}}=0$ Thus, new flow line and equipotential lines are drawn on transformed section with $\mathrm{x}$ -distance changed to $x \sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{z}}}{\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{x}}}}$ while keeping the vertical dimension constant. If we scale up the depth by keeping the horizontal distance same the depth will be scaled by factor $\sqrt{\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{x}} / \mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{z}}}$ .

questionText: A vertical trench is excavated in a clayey soil deposit having a surcharge load of $30 \mathrm{kPa}$ . A fluid of unit weight $12 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{3}$ is poured in the trench to prevent collapse as the excavation proceeds. Assume that the fluid is not seeping through the soil deposit. If the undrained cohesion of the clay deposit is $20 \mathrm{kPa}$ and saturated unit weight is $18 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{3}$ , what is the maximum depth of unsupported excavation (in $\mathrm{m}$ , rounded off to two decimal places) ? ____

questionText: Consider that a force $P$ is acting on the surface of a half-space (Boussingesq's problem). The expression for the vertical stress $\left(\sigma_{z}\right)$ at any point $(r, z)$ with the half-space is given as, $\sigma_{z}=\frac{3 P}{2 \pi} \frac{z^{3}}{\left(r^{2}+z^{2}\right)^{5 / 2}}$ where, $r$ is the radial distance, and $z$ is the depth with downward direction taken as positive. At any given $r$ , there is a variation of $\sigma_{z}$ along $z$ , and at a specific $z$ , the value of $\sigma_{z}$ will be maximum. What is the locus of the maximum $\sigma_{z}$ ?

explanationText: The expression for the vertical stress $\left(\sigma_{2}\right)$ at any point $(r, z)$ with the half-space is given as $\sigma_{z}=\frac{3 P}{2 \pi} \frac{z^{3}}{\left(r^{2}+z^{2}\right)^{5 / 2}}$ For $\sigma_{\mathrm{z}}$ to be maximum $\begin{aligned} & \frac{\sigma_{z}}{\partial z}=0 \Rightarrow \frac{3 P}{2 \pi} \frac{\partial}{\partial z}\left[\frac{z^{3}}{\left(r^{2}+z^{2}\right)^{5 / 2}}\right] \\ &=\frac{3 P}{2 \pi} \frac{\left[\left(r^{2}+z^{2}\right)^{5 / 2}-z^{3} \times \frac{5}{2}\left(r^{2}+z^{2}\right)^{3 / 2} \times 2 z\right]}{\left(r^{2}+z^{2}\right)^{5}}=0 \\ &=\left[\left(r^{2}+z^{2}\right)\left(3 z^{2}\right)-5 z^{4}\right]=0 \\ &=3 r^{2}+3 z^{2}=5 z^{2} \\ & z^{2}=\frac{3 r^{2}}{2} \end{aligned}$

questionText: A drained direct shear test was carried out on a sandy soil. Under a normal stress of $50 \mathrm{kPa}$ , the test specimen field at shear stress of $35 \mathrm{kPa}$ . The angle of internal friction of the sample is ______ degree (round off to the nearest integer).

τf=35kPa \tau_{\mathrm{f}}=35 \mathrm{kPa} τf​=35kPa
For sandy soil, C=0C=0C=0
Shear stress =τf=C+σntan⁡ϕf=\tau_{f}=\mathrm{C}+\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} \tan \phi_{\mathrm{f}}=τf​=C+σn​tanϕf​
35=50tan⁡ϕfϕf=35∘ \begin{aligned} & 35=50 \tan \phi_{\mathrm{f}} \\ & \phi_{\mathrm{f}}=35^{\circ} \end{aligned} ​35=50tanϕf​ϕf​=35∘​
explanationText: Given, $\sigma_{\mathrm{n}}=50 \mathrm{kPa}$ $\tau_{\mathrm{f}}=35 \mathrm{kPa}$ For sandy soil, $C=0$ Shear stress $=\tau_{f}=\mathrm{C}+\sigma_{\mathrm{n}} \tan \phi_{\mathrm{f}}$ $\begin{aligned} & 35=50 \tan \phi_{\mathrm{f}} \\ & \phi_{\mathrm{f}}=35^{\circ} \end{aligned}$

questionMarkup: A saturated compressible clay layer of thickness h is sandwiched between two sand layers, as shown in the figure. Initially, the total vertical stress and pore water pressure at point P, which is located at the mid-depth of the clay layer, were 150 kPa and 25 kPa, respectively. Construction of a building caused an additional total vertical stress of 100 kPa at P. When the vertical effective stress at P is 175 kPa, the percentage of consolidation in the clay layer at P is _____________. (in integer)
questionText: A saturated compressible clay layer of thickness h is sandwiched between two sand layers, as shown in the figure. Initially, the total vertical stress and pore water pressure at point P, which is located at the mid-depth of the clay layer, were 150 kPa and 25 kPa, respectively. Construction of a building caused an additional total vertical stress of 100 kPa at P. When the vertical effective stress at P is 175 kPa, the percentage of consolidation in the clay layer at P is _____________. (in integer)
explanationHtml:
Initial effective stress at P
σP1′=150−25=125kPa\sigma _{P_1}'=150-25=125kPa σP1​′​=150−25=125kPa
After construction,
σP2′=125+100=225kPa\sigma _{P_2}'=125+100=225kPa σP2​′​=125+100=225kPa
100% consolidation will occur when effective stress at P reaches 225 kPa.
Percentage of consolidation when vertical effective stress is at P is 175 kPa.
=175−125225−125×100=50100×100=50=\frac{175-125}{225-125} \times 100=\frac{50}{100} \times 100=50 =225−125175−125​×100=10050​×100=50
explanationText: Initial effective stress at P $\sigma _{P_1}'=150-25=125kPa$ After construction, $\sigma _{P_2}'=125+100=225kPa$ 100% consolidation will occur when effective stress at P reaches 225 kPa. Percentage of consolidation when vertical effective stress is at P is 175 kPa. $=\frac{175-125}{225-125} \times 100=\frac{50}{100} \times 100=50$

subject: Geotechnical Engineering
questionMarkup:
Read the following statements:

(P) While designing a shallow footing in sandy soil, monsoon season is considered for critical design in terms of bearing capacity.
(Q) For slope stability of an earthen dam, sudden drawdown is never a critical condition.
(R) In a sandy sea beach, quicksand condition can arise only if the critical hydraulic gradient exceeds the existing hydraulic gradient.
(S) The active earth thrust on a rigid retaining wall supporting homogeneous cohesionless backfill will reduce with the lowering of water table in the backfill.

Which one of the following combinations is correct?
questionText: Read the following statements: (P) While designing a shallow footing in sandy soil, monsoon season is considered for critical design in terms of bearing capacity. (Q) For slope stability of an earthen dam, sudden drawdown is never a critical condition. (R) In a sandy sea beach, quicksand condition can arise only if the critical hydraulic gradient exceeds the existing hydraulic gradient. (S) The active earth thrust on a rigid retaining wall supporting homogeneous cohesionless backfill will reduce with the lowering of water table in the backfill. Which one of the following combinations is correct?
explanationHtml:
In monsoon season sand will be fully saturated hence this will be critical condition in designing of shallow foundation.
In case of sudden drawdown flow direction reverses hence for slope stability, it will be critical condition.
In sandy sea beach, quicksand condition can arise only if existing hydraulic gradient exceeds the critical hydraulic gradient.
explanationText: In monsoon season sand will be fully saturated hence this will be critical condition in designing of shallow foundation.In case of sudden drawdown flow direction reverses hence for slope stability, it will be critical condition.In sandy sea beach, quicksand condition can arise only if existing hydraulic gradient exceeds the critical hydraulic gradient.

Take Bearing capacity factors: $N_{c}=5.14$ , $N_{q}=1.0$ , and $N_{\gamma}=0.0$ ; Shape factors: $s_{c}=1.16$ , $s_{q}=1.0$ and $s_{\gamma}=1.0$ ; Depth factors: $d_{c}=1.1$ , $d_{q}=1.0$ and $d_{\gamma}=1.0$ ; and Inclination factors: $i_{c}=1.0$ and $i_{q}=1.0$ and $i_{\gamma}=1.0$ .Using Meyerhoff's method, the load (in kN, round off to two decimal places) that can be applied on the footing with a factor of safety of 2.5 is _________________

explanationText: $\begin{aligned}& \text { Given data: } 2.8 \times 3.56, e=0.8, D_{f}=1.5 \mathrm{~m} \\ N_{c}&=5.14, \qquad N_{q}=1, \qquad N_{r}=0 \\ S_{c}&=1.16, \qquad S_{q}=1, \qquad S_{r}=1.0 \\ d_{c}&=1.1, \qquad d_{q}=1, \qquad d_{f}=1.0 \\ i_{c}&=1, \qquad \quad i_{q}=1, \qquad i_{r}=1.0 \\ \gamma&=18.2, \qquad c=40 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \\ B^{\prime}&=B-2 e_{x}=2.8-2(0.8)=1.2 \mathrm{~m} \\ L^{\prime}&=L=3.5 \end{aligned}$ Ultimate bearing capacity $\begin{aligned} q_{u} &=C N_{c} S_{c} d_{c} i_{c}+\gamma D_{p} N_{q} S_{q} d_{q} i_{q}+0.5 B^{\prime} \gamma N_{r} S_{r} d_{r} \\ q_{u} &=40 \times 5.14 \times 1.16 \times 1.1+18.2 \times 1.5 \times 1+0 \\ q_{n u} &=q_{u}-\gamma D_{f}=262.346 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \\ q_{n s} &=\frac{q_{n u}}{F}=104.938 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \end{aligned}$ $\begin{aligned} \text { Net safe load } &=q_{n s} \times A=\frac{q_{n u}}{F} \times\left(B^{\prime} \times L\right) \\ &=104.938 \times 1.2 \times 3.5 \mathrm{kN} \end{aligned}$ Load applied on the footing = 440.740 kN

\begin{aligned} q_{u} &=C N_{c} S_{c} d_{c} i_{c}+\gamma D_{p} N_{q} S_{q} d_{q} i_{q}+0.5 B^{\prime} \gamma N_{r} S_{r} d_{r} \\ q_{u} &=40 \times 5.14 \times 1.16 \times 1.1+18.2 \times 1.5 \times 1+0 \\ q_{n u} &=q_{u}-\gamma D_{f}=262.346 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \\ q_{n s} &=\frac{q_{n u}}{F}=104.938 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \end{aligned}
\begin{aligned} \text { Net safe load } &=q_{n s} \times A=\frac{q_{n u}}{F} \times\left(B^{\prime} \times L\right) \\ &=104.938 \times 1.2 \times 3.5 \mathrm{kN} \end{aligned}

questionText: A clay layer of thickness H has a preconsolidation pressure $p_{c}$ and an initial void ratio $e_{0}$ .The initial effective overburden stress at the mid-height of the layer is $p_{0}$ . At the same location, the increment in effective stress due to applied external load is $\Delta p$ . The compression and swelling indices of the clay are $C_{c}$ and $C_{s}$ , respectively. If $p_{0} \lt p_{c} \lt \left(p_{0}+\Delta p\right)$ , then the correct expression to estimate the consolidation settlement $\left(S_{c}\right)$ of the clay layer is

As the soil is initially in over consolidate state (po<pc)(p_o \lt p_c)(po​<pc​), due to the external applied load (Δp)(\Delta p)(Δp) the soil initially undergoes re-compression upto (pc)(p_c)(pc​) and then changes to virgin compression from (pc)(p_c)(pc​) to (pf)(p_f)(pf​)

The re-compression index (Cr)(C_r)(Cr​) is also called Swelling index, (CS)(C_S)(CS​).

explanationText: As the soil is initially in over consolidate state $(p_o \lt p_c)$ , due to the external applied load $(\Delta p)$ the soil initially undergoes re-compression upto $(p_c)$ and then changes to virgin compression from $(p_c)$ to $(p_f)$ The re-compression index $(C_r)$ is also called Swelling index, $(C_S)$ . $s_{c}=\frac{H}{I+e_{0}} \left[C_{s} \log \frac{p_{c}}{p_{0}}+C_{c} \log \frac{p_{0}+\Delta p}{p_{c}}\right]$

Considering the trail slip circle KLM, the factor of the safety against the failure of slope under undrained condition (round off to two decimal places) is ___________
questionText: An unsupported slope of height 15 m is shown in the figure (not to scale), in which the slope face makes an angle $50^{\circ}$ with the horizontal. The slope material comprises purely cohesive soil having undrained cohesion 75 kPa. A trial slip circle KLM, with a radius 25 m, passes through the crest and toe of the slope and it subtends an angle $60^{\circ}$ at its center O. The weight of the active soil mass (W, bounded by KLMN) is 2500 kN/m, which is acting at a horizontal distance of 10 m from the toe of the slope. Consider the water table to be present at a very large depth from the ground surface.Considering the trail slip circle KLM, the factor of the safety against the failure of slope under undrained condition (round off to two decimal places) is ___________

questionText: The soil profile at a construction site is shown in the figure (not to scale). Ground water table (GWT) is at 5 m below the ground level at present. An old well data shows that the ground water table was as low as 10 m below the ground level in the past. Take unit weight of water, $\gamma_{W}=9.81 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{3}$ .The overconsolidation ratio (OCR)(round off to two decimal places) at the mid-point of the clay layer is _______
explanationHtml: OCR=σˉcσˉ0σˉc= Preconsolidation stress σˉ0= Present effective stress σˉc=17.5×10+(18.5−9.81)×5+(17−9.81)×4=247.21kN/m2σˉ0=17.5×5+(18.5−9.81)×10+(17−9.81)×4=203.16kN/m2OCR=247.21203.16=1.22\begin{aligned} \mathrm{OCR} &=\frac{\bar{\sigma}_{c}}{\bar{\sigma}_{0}} \\ \bar{\sigma}_{c} &=\text { Preconsolidation stress } \\ \bar{\sigma}_{0} &=\text { Present effective stress } \\ \bar{\sigma}_{c} &=17.5 \times 10+(18.5-9.81) \times 5+(17-9.81) \times 4 \\ &=247.21 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \\ \bar{\sigma}_{0} &=17.5 \times 5+(18.5-9.81) \times 10+(17-9.81) \times 4 \\ &=203.16 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \\ \mathrm{OCR} &=\frac{247.21}{203.16}=1.22 \end{aligned}OCRσˉc​σˉ0​σˉc​σˉ0​OCR​=σˉ0​σˉc​​= Preconsolidation stress = Present effective stress =17.5×10+(18.5−9.81)×5+(17−9.81)×4=247.21kN/m2=17.5×5+(18.5−9.81)×10+(17−9.81)×4=203.16kN/m2=203.16247.21​=1.22​
explanationText: $\begin{aligned} \mathrm{OCR} &=\frac{\bar{\sigma}_{c}}{\bar{\sigma}_{0}} \\ \bar{\sigma}_{c} &=\text { Preconsolidation stress } \\ \bar{\sigma}_{0} &=\text { Present effective stress } \\ \bar{\sigma}_{c} &=17.5 \times 10+(18.5-9.81) \times 5+(17-9.81) \times 4 \\ &=247.21 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \\ \bar{\sigma}_{0} &=17.5 \times 5+(18.5-9.81) \times 10+(17-9.81) \times 4 \\ &=203.16 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{2} \\ \mathrm{OCR} &=\frac{247.21}{203.16}=1.22 \end{aligned}$

questionText: The cohesion (c), angle of internal friction $(\phi)$ and unit weight $(\gamma)$ of a soil are $15 \mathrm{kPa}, 20^{\circ}$ and $17.5 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{3}$ , respectively. The maximum depth of unsupported excavation in the soil (in m, round off to two decimal places) is __________
explanationHtml:
Maximum depth of unsupported excavation,
H=4Cγtkaka=1−sin⁡ϕ1+sin⁡ϕ=1−sin⁡20∘1+sin⁡20∘=0.49⇒H=4×1517.50.49=4.9 m\begin{aligned} H&=\frac{4 C}{\gamma_{t} \sqrt{k_{a}}} \\ k_{a}&=\frac{1-\sin \phi}{1+\sin \phi}=\frac{1-\sin 20^{\circ}}{1+\sin 20^{\circ}}=0.49 \\ \Rightarrow \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad H&=\frac{4 \times 15}{17.5 \sqrt{0.49}}=4.9 \mathrm{~m} \end{aligned}Hka​⇒H​=γt​ka​​4C​=1+sinϕ1−sinϕ​=1+sin20∘1−sin20∘​=0.49=17.50.49​4×15​=4.9 m​
explanationText: Maximum depth of unsupported excavation, $\begin{aligned} H&=\frac{4 C}{\gamma_{t} \sqrt{k_{a}}} \\ k_{a}&=\frac{1-\sin \phi}{1+\sin \phi}=\frac{1-\sin 20^{\circ}}{1+\sin 20^{\circ}}=0.49 \\ \Rightarrow \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad H&=\frac{4 \times 15}{17.5 \sqrt{0.49}}=4.9 \mathrm{~m} \end{aligned}$

The specific gravity of soil solids is 2.65 and unit weight of water is $9.81 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{3}$ . The unit weight of the soil sample on full saturation is

explanationHtml: w=0.25,γt=18.5kN/m3Gs=2.65,γw=9.81γt=GSγW(1+w)1+e⇒e=2.65×9.81×1.2518.5−1⇒e=0.756At full saturation,S=1⇒γsat=(GS+e)γW1+eγsat =(2.65+0.756)×9.811.756=19.03kN/m3\begin{aligned} \mathrm{w} &=0.25, \gamma_{\mathrm{t}}=18.5 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{3} \\ \mathrm{G}_{\mathrm{s}} &=2.65, \gamma_{\mathrm{w}}=9.81 \\ \gamma_{\mathrm{t}} &=\frac{G_{\mathrm{S}} \gamma_{W}(1+w)}{1+e} \\ \Rightarrow \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \mathrm{e} &=\frac{2.65 \times 9.81 \times 1.25}{18.5}-1\\ \Rightarrow \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad e&=0.756\\ \text{At full saturation}, \quad \mathrm{S}&=1\\ \Rightarrow \qquad \qquad \qquad \quad \gamma_{\mathrm{sat}}&=\frac{\left(G_{\mathrm{S}}+e\right) \gamma_{\mathrm{W}}}{1+e}\\ \gamma_{\text {sat }} &=\frac{(2.65+0.756) \times 9.81}{1.756} \\ &=19.03 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{3} \end{aligned}wGs​γt​⇒e⇒eAt full saturation,S⇒γsat​γsat ​​=0.25,γt​=18.5kN/m3=2.65,γw​=9.81=1+eGS​γW​(1+w)​=18.52.65×9.81×1.25​−1=0.756=1=1+e(GS​+e)γW​​=1.756(2.65+0.756)×9.81​=19.03kN/m3​
explanationText: $\begin{aligned} \mathrm{w} &=0.25, \gamma_{\mathrm{t}}=18.5 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{3} \\ \mathrm{G}_{\mathrm{s}} &=2.65, \gamma_{\mathrm{w}}=9.81 \\ \gamma_{\mathrm{t}} &=\frac{G_{\mathrm{S}} \gamma_{W}(1+w)}{1+e} \\ \Rightarrow \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \mathrm{e} &=\frac{2.65 \times 9.81 \times 1.25}{18.5}-1\\ \Rightarrow \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad e&=0.756\\ \text{At full saturation}, \quad \mathrm{S}&=1\\ \Rightarrow \qquad \qquad \qquad \quad \gamma_{\mathrm{sat}}&=\frac{\left(G_{\mathrm{S}}+e\right) \gamma_{\mathrm{W}}}{1+e}\\ \gamma_{\text {sat }} &=\frac{(2.65+0.756) \times 9.81}{1.756} \\ &=19.03 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{3} \end{aligned}$

questionText: A constant head permeability test was conducted on a soil specimen under a hydraulic gradient of 2.5. The soil specimen has specific gravity of 2.65 and saturated water content of 20%. If the coefficient of permeability of the soil is 0.1 cm/s, the seepage velocity (in cm/s, round off to two decimal places) through the soil specimen is ________.
explanationHtml: Void ratio,  e=wGs=0.2×2.651=0.53Porosity,  n=e1+e=0.3464Seepage velocity,  Vs=vn=kin=0.1×2.50.3464=0.72cm/sec\begin{aligned} \text{Void ratio,}\; e&=\frac{wG}{s}\\ &=\frac{0.2 \times 2.65}{1}=0.53\\ \text{Porosity,}\; n&=\frac{e}{1+e}=0.3464\\ \text{Seepage velocity,}\; V_s&=\frac{v}{n}=\frac{k_i}{n}\\ &=\frac{0.1 \times 2.5}{0.3464}=0.72 cm/sec \end{aligned}Void ratio,ePorosity,nSeepage velocity,Vs​​=swG​=10.2×2.65​=0.53=1+ee​=0.3464=nv​=nki​​=0.34640.1×2.5​=0.72cm/sec​
explanationText: $\begin{aligned} \text{Void ratio,}\; e&=\frac{wG}{s}\\ &=\frac{0.2 \times 2.65}{1}=0.53\\ \text{Porosity,}\; n&=\frac{e}{1+e}=0.3464\\ \text{Seepage velocity,}\; V_s&=\frac{v}{n}=\frac{k_i}{n}\\ &=\frac{0.1 \times 2.5}{0.3464}=0.72 cm/sec \end{aligned}$
explanationTex: \begin{aligned} \text{Void ratio,}\; e&=\frac{wG}{s}\\ &=\frac{0.2 \times 2.65}{1}=0.53\\ \text{Porosity,}\; n&=\frac{e}{1+e}=0.3464\\ \text{Seepage velocity,}\; V_s&=\frac{v}{n}=\frac{k_i}{n}\\ &=\frac{0.1 \times 2.5}{0.3464}=0.72 cm/sec \end{aligned}

questionText: A 10 m thick clay layer is resting over a 3 m thick sand layer and is submerged. questionText: A square footing of 2 m sides rests on the surface of a homogeneous soil bed having the properties: cohesion c=24 kPa, angle of internal friction $\phi =25^{\circ}$ , and unit weight $\gamma =18kN/m^3$ . Terzaghi's bearing capacity factors for $\phi =25^{\circ}$ are $N_c=25.1, N_q=12.7$ , $N_{\gamma}=9.7, N_c'=14.8,N_q'=5.6$ , and $N_{\gamma}'=3.2$ . The ultimate bearing capacity of the foundation (in kPa, round off to 2 decimal places) is _______

questionMarkup:
For the following statements:

P: The lateral stress in the  soil while being tested in an oedometer is always at-rest.
Q: For a perfectly rigid strip footing at deeper depths in a sand deposit, the vertical normal contact stress at the footing edge is greater than that at its centre.
R: The corrections for overburden pressure and dilatancy are not applied to measured SPT-N values in case of clay deposits.

The correct combination of the statements is
questionText: For the following statements:P: The lateral stress in the soil while being tested in an oedometer is always at-rest. Q: For a perfectly rigid strip footing at deeper depths in a sand deposit, the vertical normal contact stress at the footing edge is greater than that at its centre. R: The corrections for overburden pressure and dilatancy are not applied to measured SPT-N values in case of clay deposits.The correct combination of the statements is
explanationHtml:
P: True
In the Oedometer test, stress is applied to the soil specimen along the vertical axis, while strain in the horizontal direction is prevented by the confining ring (a condition of zero lateral strain). Thus it simulates at-rest condition.

Q: True
For a perfectly rigid footing resting on surface of sand deposit, the contact pressure distribution is zero at the edges and maximum at centre. However, for a very deep rigid footing on sand, the contact pressure distribution may tend to become like that of rigid footing on clayey soil, with edge contact stress greater than at its centre.

R: True
For cohesive soil, there is no need for overburden pressure correction (Peck et al 1974). For cohesionless soil at first overburden pressure correction is made, then if it is fine sand or silt under water table with N-value >\gt> 15, dilatancy correction is made.

questionText: The void ratio of a soil is 0.55 at an effective normal stress of 140 kPa. The compression index of the soil is 0.25. In order to reduce the void ratio to 0.4, an increase in the magnitude of effective normal stress (in kPa, up to one decimal place) should be ______

explanationText: $\begin{aligned} \Delta H &=\frac{H_{0} \Delta e}{1+e_{0}}=\frac{H_{0} C_{c}}{1+e_{0}} \log \left(\frac{\sigma_{0}+\Delta \sigma}{\sigma_{0}}\right) \\ \Delta H &=H_{0}\left(\frac{0.55-0.40}{1+0.50}\right)=\frac{H_{0} \times 0.25}{1+0.50} \log \left(\frac{140+\Delta \sigma}{140}\right) \\ \frac{0.15}{0.25} &=\frac{3}{5}=\log \left(\frac{140+\Delta \sigma}{140}\right) \\ \Delta \sigma &=417.35 \mathrm{kPa} \end{aligned}$

explanationText: $\begin{aligned} C_{u}=& 50 \mathrm{kPa}, \gamma=18 \mathrm{kN} / \mathrm{m}^{3}, \mathrm{FOS}=2 \\ Q_{\text {up}}=& 9 \mathrm{C} \times B^{2}+\alpha \bar{C}(4 \mathrm{BL})=1000 \mathrm{kN} \\ 1000=& 9 \times 50 \times 0.5 \times 0.5+0.75 \\ & \times 50(4 \times 0.5 \mathrm{L}) \\ L=& 11.83 \mathrm{m} \end{aligned}$

explanationText: Dry soil mass =88 gm Volume of dry soil = 50 cc Dry density of soil mass, $\begin{aligned} \rho_{d}&=\frac{M_{d}}{V_{d}}=\frac{88}{50} \mathrm{gm} / \mathrm{cc}\\ \therefore \text{ Shrinkage limit, } w_{s}&=\frac{1}{R}-\frac{1}{G}=\frac{1}{\left(\rho_{d} / \rho_{w}\right)}-\frac{1}{G} \\ w_{s} &=\frac{\rho_{w}}{\rho_{d}}-\frac{1}{G} \\ &=\frac{1}{1.76}-\frac{1}{2.71}=0.1990 \end{aligned}$

explanationText: For strip footing on sand (c=0) $q_{u}=\gamma D_{f} N_{q}+0.5 \mathrm{B} \gamma N_{\gamma}$ In flooding condition water level rises to base of footing hence IIIrd term unit weight of soil will change and IInd term unit weight will be unaffected. $\begin{array}{ll} \therefore & q_{u}=\gamma D_{f} N_{q}+0.5 B \gamma N_{\gamma} \\ \because & \gamma \simeq \frac{1}{2} \gamma_{s a t} \end{array}$ Hence third term reduced and second term will be same thereby percentage reduction will not be 50%. Undrained shear strength.

=c+σˉntan⁡ϕ′τ=20+76.76tan⁡18∘50=0.9788 \begin{aligned} &=\frac{c+\bar{\sigma}_{n} \tan \phi^{\prime}}{\tau} \\ &=\frac{20+76.76 \tan 18^{\circ}}{50}=0.9788 \end{aligned}​=τc+σˉn​tanϕ′​=5020+76.76tan18∘​=0.9788​

explanationText: The point bearing resistance of piles in sandy soils $Q_P=A_b\ \cdot \sigma '_v \cdot N_q$ As the area at base $(A_b)$ and $N_q$ are same for both the piles given, $Q_P \propto \sigma '_v$ For dry sand condition, $\sigma '_v=\sigma _v=20 \times \gamma$ For submerged condition, $\sigma '_v=20 \times \gamma '$ $\begin{aligned} \text{Since, } \gamma '&= \frac{1}{2} \gamma \\ \therefore \;\; QP_2&\approx \frac{1}{2} QP_1\\ QP_1& \approx QP_2 \end{aligned}$ Therefore, $QP_1 \gt QP_2$ by about 100%.

questionMarkup: A consolidated undrained CUˉ\bar{CU}CUˉ triaxial compression test is conducted on a normally consolidated clay at a confining pressure of 100 kPa. questionText: A consolidated undrained $\bar{CU}$ triaxial compression test is conducted on a normally consolidated clay at a confining pressure of 100 kPa. The deviator stress at failure is 80 kPa, and the pore-water pressure measured at failure is 50 kPa. The effective angle of internalfriction (in degrees, up to one decimal place) of the soil is _________
explanationHtml:
CU test is conducted.
σ3=100kPa,σa=80kPa,u=50kPaσ1=σ3+σd=100+80=180kPaσˉ1=σ1−u=180−50=130kPaσˉ3=σ3−u=100−50=50kPaσˉ1=σˉ3tan⁡2(45+ϕ′2)+2C′tan⁡(45+ϕ′2)Assume C′=0σˉ1=σˉ3tan⁡2(45+ϕ′2)130=50tan⁡2(45+ϕ′2)ϕ′=26.4∘ \begin{aligned} \sigma_{3}= 100 &\mathrm{kPa}, \sigma_{a}=80 \mathrm{kPa}, u=50 \mathrm{kPa} \\ \sigma_{1}&=\sigma_{3}+\sigma_{d} =100+80=180 \mathrm{kPa} \\ \bar{\sigma}_{1}&=\sigma_{1}-u= 180-50=130 \mathrm{kPa}\\ \bar{\sigma}_{3}&=\sigma_{3}-u=100-50=50 \mathrm{kPa} \\ \bar{\sigma}_{1}&=\bar{\sigma}_{3} \tan ^{2}\left(45+\frac{\phi^{\prime}}{2}\right)+2 C^{\prime} \tan \left(45+\frac{\phi^{\prime}}{2}\right) \\ \text{Assume }\quad C^{\prime}&=0 \\ \bar{\sigma}_{1}&=\bar{\sigma}_{3} \tan ^{2}\left(45+\frac{\phi^{\prime}}{2}\right) \\ 130&=50 \tan ^{2}\left(45+\frac{\phi^{\prime}}{2}\right) \\ \phi^{\prime}&=26.4^{\circ} \end{aligned}σ3​=100σ1​σˉ1​σˉ3​σˉ1​Assume C′σˉ1​130ϕ′​kPa,σa​=80kPa,u=50kPa=σ3​+σd​=100+80=180kPa=σ1​−u=180−50=130kPa=σ3​−u=100−50=50kPa=σˉ3​tan2(45+2ϕ′​)+2C′tan(45+2ϕ′​)=0=σˉ3​tan2(45+2ϕ′​)=50tan2(45+2ϕ′​)=26.4∘​
explanationText: CU test is conducted. $\begin{aligned} \sigma_{3}= 100 &\mathrm{kPa}, \sigma_{a}=80 \mathrm{kPa}, u=50 \mathrm{kPa} \\ \sigma_{1}&=\sigma_{3}+\sigma_{d} =100+80=180 \mathrm{kPa} \\ \bar{\sigma}_{1}&=\sigma_{1}-u= 180-50=130 \mathrm{kPa}\\ \bar{\sigma}_{3}&=\sigma_{3}-u=100-50=50 \mathrm{kPa} \\ \bar{\sigma}_{1}&=\bar{\sigma}_{3} \tan ^{2}\left(45+\frac{\phi^{\prime}}{2}\right)+2 C^{\prime} \tan \left(45+\frac{\phi^{\prime}}{2}\right) \\ \text{Assume }\quad C^{\prime}&=0 \\ \bar{\sigma}_{1}&=\bar{\sigma}_{3} \tan ^{2}\left(45+\frac{\phi^{\prime}}{2}\right) \\ 130&=50 \tan ^{2}\left(45+\frac{\phi^{\prime}}{2}\right) \\ \phi^{\prime}&=26.4^{\circ} \end{aligned}$

questionText: A 3 m thick clay layer is subjected to an initial uniform pore pressure of 145 kPa as shown in the figure. For the given ground conditions, the time (in days, rounded to the nearest integer) required for 90% consolidation would be ____________

As per Terzaghi's 1-D consolidation theory
